title: Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì
binary_signature: I I / I I / II II / I I
cosmological_meaning: Perseverance, spiritual initiation, conquest of death
description: Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì is the #14 major chapter (Ojú Odù) of the sacred 256 Odù Ifá corpus, governing perseverance, spiritual initiation, conquest of death.
etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from 'Ì-rẹ-tẹ̀' ('The act of stepping upon and subduing adversity' or 'Pressing upon the earth to extract vital healing'). Metaphysically, it signifies botanical renewal, stepping victoriously upon affliction, and the revival of life out of decay. Governs cosmic forces of plant intelligence, regenerative chemistry, and earthly healing. In moral philosophy, it mandates Ìwà-rere through unshakeable resilience in sickness, dedication to healing fellow humans, ethical handling of potent natural forces, and stepping forward courageously.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Origins (c. Primordial–11th Century CE): Manifested at primordial Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the divine science of Osanyin (botanical medicine), herbal transmutation, and stepping victoriously upon adversity. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ & Regional Kingdoms (c. 14th–19th Century CE): Consulted by the royal physicians and guild herbalists of Old Ọ̀yọ́ before administering complex remedies and treating war wounds; consulted during Babaláwo forest initiations (Ìtẹfá) to consecrate new seers. Transatlantic Diaspora Survival: Maintained in Cuba and Brazil as the premier Odù presiding over the sacred Omiero herbal wash and the consecration of the Babaláwo priesthood in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá. Contemporary Era & UNESCO Heritage: Documented in international botanical and ethnographic compendiums as an apex repository of indigenous African pharmacology and regenerative medicine.
material_and_craftsmanship: Chiseled onto Ọpọ́n Ifá carved from durable Ọmọ timber, featuring intricate leaf and vine relief carvings intertwined around the rim. Sifted with pure Ìyẹ̀ròsùn dust. Employs 16 consecrated Ikin palm nuts, an emerald-tinted or brass Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, and a carved bone or bronze Ìrókẹ́ sculpted with an herbalist carrying a staff of leaves.
social_and_ritual_context: Priests wear pure white textiles accented with fresh herbal-green sashes. Prescribes cooling propitiations (Ẹbọ Ẹrọ) such as guinea fowl (Ẹtù), snails, shea butter, and freshly steeped forest leaves in cold spring water to heal stubborn physical sickness and renew weary spirits. Crucial in Babaláwo consecrations (Ìtẹfá), forest medicine rites, and purifying communal sanctuaries, while strictly safeguarding pharmacological formulas.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì tẹ ikú lórí, ó tẹ àrùn mọ́lẹ̀; ẹni tí Òrìṣà tì lẹ́yìn kì í tẹ́. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì tramples death beneath its feet and crushes infirmity into the earth; he whom the Divinities support shall never be disgraced — Affirming absolute victory over existential affliction through divine spiritual backing.)

Bí a bá tẹ ilẹ̀ kankan, ilẹ̀ a gbè wá; àìbẹ̀rù ni kókó ìṣẹ́gun. (If we tread firmly upon the earth, the earth will sustain and elevate us; absolute fearlessness is the cornerstone of triumph — Teaching grounded self-assurance and harmony with physical reality.)

Ewé kì í jẹ́ kí igbó kú; ìmọ̀ ewé ni àṣírí ìwòsàn gbogbo ayé. (Leaves never allow the forest to perish; the knowledge of plants is the secret key to universal healing — Celebrating nature's endless capacity for biological and spiritual regeneration.)
diaspora_connections: Celebrated in Afro-Cuban Lucumí as Irete Meji, recorded in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá under Osanyin and Obatala, central to the brewing of the sacred Omiero herbal bath and the initiation of the Babalawo. In Brazilian Candomblé Ketu, Iretê is the 16-cowrie sign in the Merindilogún associated with the sacred leaves (Folhas / Ewé) of Osanyin, physical rejuvenation, and overcoming fatal diseases. In the Caribbean, it represents healing and botanical authority.
media_production_notes: Visual lighting palette: Deep forest green (#1B4332), leafy viridian (#2D6A4F), and sparkling dew-drop amber reflections (#D4A373). Camera choreography: Low, gliding tracking shot brushing gently across wild medicinal leaves toward the centered Ọpọ́n Ifá. Audio design: Gentle sound of rain falling on broad tropical leaves, rhythmic stirring of liquid in an earthenware pot, chirping cicadas, and low-frequency resonant chanting.

In moral philosophy, it mandates Ìwà-rere through unshakeable resilience in sickness, dedication to healing fellow humans, ethical handling of potent natural forces, and stepping forward courageously.
details.material_and_craftsmanship: Chiseled onto Ọpọ́n Ifá carved from durable Ọmọ timber, featuring intricate leaf and vine relief carvings intertwined around the rim. Sifted with pure Ìyẹ̀ròsùn dust. Employs 16 consecrated Ikin palm nuts, an emerald-tinted or brass Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, and a carved bone or bronze Ìrókẹ́ sculpted with an herbalist carrying a staff of leaves.
details.social_and_ritual_context: Priests wear pure white textiles accented with fresh herbal-green sashes. Prescribes cooling propitiations (Ẹbọ Ẹrọ) such as guinea fowl (Ẹtù), snails, shea butter, and freshly steeped forest leaves in cold spring water to heal stubborn physical sickness and renew weary spirits. Crucial in Babaláwo consecrations (Ìtẹfá), forest medicine rites, and purifying communal sanctuaries, while strictly safeguarding pharmacological formulas.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì tẹ ikú lórí, ó tẹ àrùn mọ́lẹ̀; ẹni tí Òrìṣà tì lẹ́yìn kì í tẹ́. (Ìrẹtẹ̀ Méjì tramples death beneath its feet and crushes infirmity into the earth; he whom the Divinities support shall never be disgraced — Affirming absolute victory over existential affliction through divine spiritual backing.)

Bí a bá tẹ ilẹ̀ kankan, ilẹ̀ a gbè wá; àìbẹ̀rù ni kókó ìṣẹ́gun. (If we tread firmly upon the earth, the earth will sustain and elevate us; absolute fearlessness is the cornerstone of triumph — Teaching grounded self-assurance and harmony with physical reality.)

Ewé kì í jẹ́ kí igbó kú; ìmọ̀ ewé ni àṣírí ìwòsàn gbogbo ayé. (Leaves never allow the forest to perish; the knowledge of plants is the secret key to universal healing — Celebrating nature's endless capacity for biological and spiritual regeneration.)
details.diaspora_connections: Celebrated in Afro-Cuban Lucumí as Irete Meji, recorded in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá under Osanyin and Obatala, central to the brewing of the sacred Omiero herbal bath and the initiation of the Babalawo. In Brazilian Candomblé Ketu, Iretê is the 16-cowrie sign in the Merindilogún associated with the sacred leaves (Folhas / Ewé) of Osanyin, physical rejuvenation, and overcoming fatal diseases. In the Caribbean, it represents healing and botanical authority.
details.media_production_notes: Visual lighting palette: Deep forest green (#1B4332), leafy viridian (#2D6A4F), and sparkling dew-drop amber reflections (#D4A373). Camera choreography: Low, gliding tracking shot brushing gently across wild medicinal leaves toward the centered Ọpọ́n Ifá. Audio design: Gentle sound of rain falling on broad tropical leaves, rhythmic stirring of liquid in an earthenware pot, chirping cicadas, and low-frequency resonant chanting.

title: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì
binary_signature: I I / II II / I I / II II
cosmological_meaning: Aesthetic beauty, sweet victories, artistic abundance
description: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì is the #15 major chapter (Ojú Odù) of the sacred 256 Odù Ifá corpus, governing aesthetic beauty, sweet victories, artistic abundance.
etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from 'Ọ̀ṣẹ́' ('The sacred victory / aesthetic adornment / the sweet cleansing'). Metaphysically, it signifies the flowing freshwater river, golden honey, magnetic attraction, and triumph achieved through charm and artistic refinement rather than brutal force. Governs cosmic forces of sweet waters, maternal affection, artistic beauty, and financial victory. In moral philosophy, it mandates Ìwà-rere through sweet-tempered generosity, pristine personal hygiene, cultivating outer and inner beauty, and easing communal distress through laughter and grace.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Origins (c. Primordial–11th Century CE): Manifested at ancient Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the divine manifestation of freshwater fertility, aesthetic refinement (Ẹwà), musical elegance, and the golden sweetness of Ọ̀ṣun. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ & Regional Kingdoms (c. 14th–19th Century CE): Celebrated across the royal courts of Ọ̀yọ́, Òṣogbo, and Ìjẹ̀bú; performed during royal annual festivals with the joyous Ọ̀ṣẹ́ dance by queens, brass-smiths, and river priestesses to attract communal prosperity. Transatlantic Diaspora Survival: Maintained with dazzling beauty across Cuba and Brazil as the undisputed sign of Oshun / Oxum, maternal sweetness, gold, and financial triumph in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá. Contemporary Era & UNESCO Heritage: Acclaimed in African art theory and UNESCO World Heritage documentation as the aesthetic fountainhead of Yorùbá philosophy and sensory celebration.
material_and_craftsmanship: Carved onto luminous Ọpọ́n Ifá sculpted from honey-toned Ọmọ timber, bordered by detailed relief carvings of freshwater fish, brass mirrors, and fans. Sifted with radiant Ìyẹ̀ròsùn dust. Employs 16 smooth Ikin palm nuts, a glittering polished brass Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, and a cast-brass or carved ivory Ìrókẹ́ with polished mirror insets.
social_and_ritual_context: Priests wear glorious amber, canary yellow, and gold-trimmed lace ceremonial fabrics. Prescribes cooling propitiations (Ẹbọ Ẹrọ) such as wild forest honey, cinnamon, sweet oranges, white hens, and yellow cowries to sweeten bitter life conditions and summon financial elevation. Prime sign consulted for fertility issues, finding love, overcoming melancholy, and consecrating fine art guilds, keeping intimate shrine protocols sacred.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì, omi tútù tó ń pa iná ìbànújẹ́; ẹwà inú ni ẹ̀ṣọ́ tòótọ́. (Ọ̀ṣẹ́ Méjì, the refreshing cool waters that quench the fierce blaze of sorrow; internal character is the true aesthetic jewel of existence — Demonstrating that moral beauty and emotional tranquility outshine superficial adornments.)

Oyin kì í korò lẹ́nu ẹni tó ń lá a; ọ̀rọ̀ dídùn ń yí ìbínú padà sí ẹ̀rín. (Honey never tastes bitter on the tongue of the one who partakes of it; sweet and gentle speech transforms blazing wrath into radiant laughter — Championing the peacemaking power of gentleness and graciousness.)

Ẹni tó bá nífẹ̀ẹ́ Òrìṣà a rí oore gbà; omi tútù ní ń wẹ ìdọ̀tí ayé nù. (He who loves the Divinities with a glad heart will receive boundless goodness; pure cool water alone washes away the stains of earthly toil — Celebrating spiritual purity and joy.)
diaspora_connections: Revered throughout Afro-Cuban Lucumí as Baba Oche Meji, celebrated in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá as the personal odu of Oshun, bringing abundance, aesthetic genius, intuition, and financial triumph. In Brazilian Candomblé Ketu, Oxé is the 16-cowrie sign in the Merindilogún associated with Oxum, golden honey, maternal fertility, and artistic elegance. In Trinidad and across the Caribbean, it represents river blessings and feminine victory.
media_production_notes: Visual lighting palette: Warm liquid amber (#E09F3E), luminous canary gold (#FFF3B0), and sparkling turquoise water reflections (#48CAE4). Camera choreography: Graceful, swirling camera track floating across ripples of water reflecting sunlight upon the tray. Audio design: Splashing river currents, crystalline tinkling of brass bells, joyous female polyphonic laughter, and soft rhythmic shekere rattles.

title: Òfún Méjì
binary_signature: II II / I I / II II / I I
cosmological_meaning: Divine source, supreme purity, miracle of resurrection
description: Òfún Méjì is the #16 major chapter (Ojú Odù) of the sacred 256 Odù Ifá corpus, governing divine source, supreme purity, miracle of resurrection.
etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from 'Ẹfun' (the sacred white chalk of creation, purity, and cooling) and 'Òfún' ('The giver of boundless breath and life'). Metaphysically, it signifies the cosmic womb, primordial silence before creation, and the ultimate matrix from which all existence emerges. Governs cosmic forces of absolute purity, sacred white chalk, and miraculous manifestation. In moral philosophy, it mandates Ìwà-rere through supreme humility, meticulous adherence to spiritual taboos (Èèwọ̀), reverence for the mysteries of life, and avoiding greed and ostentatious display.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Origins (c. Primordial–11th Century CE): Revered in ancient Ilé-Ifẹ̀ as the primordial cosmic womb, the senior mother who gave birth to all sixteen Odù, and the supreme mystery of divine creation. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ & Regional Kingdoms (c. 14th–19th Century CE): Held in profound, solemn awe across the Ọ̀yọ́ Empire and regional kingdoms; spoken of only with reverent euphemisms ('Ọ̀ràngún' or 'Ẹ̀pà') during courtly divination to prevent cosmic disruption, and consulted during paramount dynastic crises. Transatlantic Diaspora Survival: Retained unbroken sanctity across Cuba and Brazil with identical reverent taboos, recognized as the mother of the Odù in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá and Candomblé Ketu. Contemporary Era & UNESCO Heritage: Acknowledged in comparative religion and UNESCO documentation as the sublime alpha-and-omega of Ifá cosmology, representing the ultimate triumph of purity.
material_and_craftsmanship: Carved onto sublime Ọpọ́n Ifá from ancient resonant timber, decorated with subtle crescent moons, eggs, and white chalk markings along the perimeter. Sifted with pure Ìyẹ̀ròsùn blended with powdered Ẹfun. Employs 16 consecrated Ikin palm nuts, a shimmering silver or mother-of-pearl Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, and a pristine ivory Ìrókẹ́ sculpted with an expectant mother holding a sacred vessel.
social_and_ritual_context: Priests wear unblemished, brilliant white robes (Aṣọ Funfun). Prescribes cooling propitiations (Ẹbọ Ẹrọ) including sixteen white river snails (Ìgbín), powdered white chalk (Ẹfun), shea butter (Orí), and cold well-water to cool heated destinies and bring miraculous breakthroughs. Consulted during profound existential crises, sovereign consecrations, and barrenness, while strictly enforcing sacred taboos and zero exposure of sanctuary secrets.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Òfún Méjì, baba gbogbo odù, ìyá tó bí ìmọ́lẹ̀; ẹni tó bá bọ̀wọ̀ fún èèwọ̀ kò ní rí ìjàmbá. (Òfún Méjì, father of all sacred chapters, the primordial mother who gave birth to cosmic light; he who strictly observes spiritual taboos shall never encounter calamity — Teaching that spiritual integrity and moral boundaries ensure divine preservation.)

Ẹfun ló ń pa orúkọ àrùn rẹ́; funfun tútù ni àṣírí àlàáfíà tòótọ́. (It is the sacred white chalk that erases the stigma of disease; pristine, cooling whiteness is the secret foundation of enduring tranquility — Praising unblemished spiritual purity as the supreme healing agent.)

A kì í fi orúkọ Òfún dárò láì bọ̀wọ̀; ẹni tó fọwọ́ mọ́ a jẹ ogún àìkú. (One does not speak the name of Òfún lightly without deep reverence; he whose hands are clean shall inherit the blessing of immortality — Warning against spiritual carelessness and championing pristine moral virtue.)
diaspora_connections: Venerated in Afro-Cuban Lucumí as Baba Ofun Meji (Orangún), recorded in the Tratado Enciclopédico de Ifá under Oduduwa and Obatala as the mother of all Odù, renowned for generating miracles out of impossibility while demanding strict white clothing and clean living. In Brazilian Candomblé Ketu, Ofún is the 16-cowrie sign in the Merindilogún associated with Oxalá, cosmic peace, and deep ancestral respect. In Caribbean Orisha traditions, it signifies transcendent blessings.
media_production_notes: Visual lighting palette: Luminous alabaster white (#FFFFFF), pearlescent silver (#E0E1DD), and soft lunar mist. Camera choreography: Transcendent slow pedestal-up shot rising majestically, then gently tilting down to reveal the entire consecrated circle of the Ọpọ́n Ifá. Audio design: High ethereal crystalline chimes, deep ocean breathing cadence, and a solitary resonant ivory clapper strike slowly reverberating into profound sacred silence.

title: Ogbè Ọ̀yẹ̀kú
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is the #17 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from the pairing of Ogbè (expansion/daylight) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (containment/night/ancestral transition). It represents the dialectical truth that life and death exist in perpetual dialogue; wisdom consists of neutralizing death through ethical sacrifice and moral fortitude.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity (c. 9th–12th Century CE): Codified as the foremost composite chapter pairing primordial Light (Ogbè) with primordial Darkness and Ancestral Transition (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú). Imperial Era: Consulted in court cases involving sudden epidemics or the mysterious illness of princes. Transatlantic Preservation: Documented as Ogbe Yekun in Cuban and Brazilian Ifá archives as a master sign for averting premature death.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ọpọ́n Ifá in two distinct vertical columns: single strokes (I) on the right for Ogbè, and double strokes (II) on the left for Ọ̀yẹ̀kú. Involves consecrated black soap and sheep sacrifice.
social_and_ritual_context: Divined during existential crises where impending mortality, legal calamity, or ancestral anger threatens a household. Prescribes rituals to convert death (Ikú) into longevity (Àìkú).
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè ń yọ̀, Ọ̀yẹ̀kú ń yọ̀; Ikú kò ní rí awo gbé ṣe. (Ogbè rejoices and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú rejoices; Death shall find no power to conquer the dedicated initiate: Affirming spiritual triumph over sudden demise.)

Bí ọjọ́ bá mọ́, òkùnkùn a yẹra; ìmọ́lẹ̀ Ifá kì í jẹ́ kí awo sọnù. (When dawn breaks, darkness recedes; the radiant light of Ifá prevents the truth-seeker from losing his path: Teaching hope amidst existential dread.)

Ẹbọ la fi ń ti ikú sẹ́yìn; orí l’awo fi ń ṣẹ́gun ọ̀tá. (It is with sacrifice that death is turned aside; it is through inner consciousness that the initiate overcomes adversity: Emphasizing spiritual vigilance.)

title: Ogbè Ìwòrì
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ìwòrì.
description: Ogbè Ìwòrì is the #18 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ìwòrì on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Formed by pairing Ogbè with Ìwòrì (deep spiritual seeing and reflection). Philosophically teaches that illumination without self-examination leads to arrogance; one must look back into history to chart the righteous future.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fatunmbi, Awo Fa'lokun (1992). Iwa-Pele: Ifa Quest.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Systematized as Ogbè-Wèyìn (Ogbè Looks Back), teaching historical retrospection. Imperial Era: Consulted before long-distance trade expeditions and diplomatic missions between Ọ̀yọ́, Dahomey, and Benin. Diaspora Lineage: Preserved in Lucumí patakís as the sign of character purification and clear vision.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as I on the right and II/I/I/II on the left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Accompanied by pure spring water offerings and pigeon sacrifice.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when an individual or clan is repeating ancestral errors or suffering from obscured vision. Restores moral focus and clears slander.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè wèyìn wo ibi tí o ti wá; ẹni tó bá gbé orí kò gbọdọ̀ tẹ́. (Ogbè, look back and examine your origins; he who carries a consecrated head must never disgrace his lineage: Teaching historical accountability.)

Ojú tí ó rí iwájú gbọ́dọ̀ wo ẹ̀yìn; a kì í sáré kọjá orígun ilé. (The eyes that gaze forward must also look behind; one does not rush past the corner of the house blindly: Exhorting caution before decisive action.)
Ìwòrì fọ omi mó awo; ìmọ́ tútù ni baba ìwòsàn. (Ìwòrì cleanses the sacred water for the initiate; cool purity is the fountainhead of all healing: Prioritizing emotional calmness.)

title: Ogbè Òdí
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Òdí.
description: Ogbè Òdí is the #19 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Òdí on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Formed by Ogbè and Òdí (barrier, seal, womb, fortification). Teaches that expansive spiritual energy (Ogbè) must be contained within disciplined ethical boundaries (Òdí) to be fertile and productive.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity: Institutionalized as Ogbè-Dí or Ogbè-Káká, governing maternal protection, fertility, and fortified boundary building against enemies. Imperial Era: Consulted when establishing new town walls or consecrating civic moats (Iyara). Transatlantic Diaspora: Revered in Cuba and Brazil for resolving reproductive difficulties.
material_and_craftsmanship: Cast as I on the right and I/II/II/I on the left. Associated with protective earthen amulets, cowrie necklaces, and consecrated river water.
social_and_ritual_context: Central to women's fertility rites, shielding newborns from malevolent witchcraft, and establishing unbreachable protective enclosures for compounds.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè dí àpò, Òdí pa àbùkù mọ́; ilé tí a fi òtítọ́ dí kì í ya. (Ogbè seals the pouch, Òdí covers dishonor; a household fortified with truth never breaks apart: Teaching protective family unity.)
Bí a bá dí odi mọ́ ọ̀tá, a kì í ṣí ojúlé fún ìbàjẹ́. (When we construct a wall against the adversary, we do not leave the gateway open to corruption: Warning against moral compromise.)

Ọmọ kì í pọ́n lójú ìyá rẹ̀; Òdí ní ń da àbò bo àwọn aláìsàn. (A child never suffers neglect in the presence of its mother; it is Òdí that spreads a mantle of protection over the weak: Honoring maternal compassion.)

title: Ogbè Ìrosùn
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ìrosùn.
description: Ogbè Ìrosùn is the #20 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ìrosùn on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairing Ogbè with Ìrosùn (red camwood, lineage blood, ancestral slumber). Explores the power of ancestral genetics and warning against treachery hidden beneath smiling faces.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ogbè-Rosùn, governing ancestral remembrance, royal camwood consecration, and uncovering hidden traps. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Era: Invoked by palace heralds to test loyalty among provincial tributary governors. Diaspora Resilience: Maintained in Lucumí tradition as a major sign of victory over envious detractors.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ọpọ́n Ifá with scarlet camwood powder (Osùn) mixed into Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Uses sacrificial roosters and bronze ornaments.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when treachery, deceit, or unprovoked envy is suspected in close domestic circles. Guides initiates to honor their paternal and maternal ancestors.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè rosùn tán, ojú ọ̀tá wọ̀gbẹ́; ẹni tí a fi osùn kùn kì í tẹ́. (Ogbè has adorned itself in sacred camwood, and the enemy's gaze is cast down into the grass; he who is anointed with ancestral blessing never faces ruin: Affirming royal immunity from spite.)

A kì í fi osùn kùn kọ́lọ́mọ kí ó má dán; orí rere ní ń fa ọlá mọ́ra. (One does not rub camwood upon a child without it shining; good fortune naturally attracts royal majesty: Teaching that inner goodness radiates outward.)
Ẹni tó gbé kòtò sílẹ̀ de awo, ara rẹ̀ ni yóò wọ̀ ọ́. (He who digs a pit to snare the righteous initiate shall stumble into it himself: Enforcing karmic justice against betrayal.)

title: Ogbè Ọ̀wọ́nrín
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀wọ́nrín.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀wọ́nrín is the #21 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀wọ́nrín on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairing Ogbè with Ọ̀wọ́nrín (reversal, whirlwind, sudden scarcity). Teaches that fortune is fluid; the wise person builds savings during abundance to prepare for unexpected reversals.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fatunmbi, Awo Fa'lokun (1992). Iwa-Pele: Ifa Quest.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Wọ́nrín or Ogbè-Hunle, governing sudden fortune, economic commodity trading, and navigating scarcity. Imperial Era: Consulted by caravan merchants before crossing the Niger River. Transatlantic Survival: Preserved in Cuba as the sign of unexpected prosperity arising from adversity.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I on the right and II/II/I/I on the left. Involves sacrifices of honey, bananas, and white textiles.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast during volatile financial transitions or sudden reversals. Directs seekers to cultivate generosity, pacify market divinities (Ajé), and practice fiscal discipline.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀wọ́nrín sọ owó di púpọ̀; ẹni tó gbọ́n kì í fi ọjọ́ ọrọ̀ gbàgbé ọjọ́ ebi. (Ọ̀wọ́nrín multiplies wealth into abundance; but the wise man never forgets the days of hunger during seasons of riches: Teaching economic foresight.)

Afẹ́fẹ́ kì í fẹ́ kí ó gbé odidi ilé lọ; awo tó fẹsẹ̀ múlẹ̀ kì í ṣubú. (The whirlwind never blows so fiercely as to carry away a sound house; an initiate anchored to truth never falls: Exhorting structural stability.)

Ajé kì í wọ ilé láì ní ìwà; ẹni tí ó ní sùúrù yóò jẹ àìkú ọlá. (Wealth does not reside in a home devoid of good character; he who possesses patience shall taste everlasting honor: Conditioning wealth upon morality.)

title: Ogbè Ọ̀bàrà
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀bàrà.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀bàrà is the #22 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀bàrà on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Combines Ogbè with Ọ̀bàrà (royalty, manifestation, speaking into reality). Teaches that the tongue possesses generative power (Ọ̀rọ̀ ni àṣẹ); speech must remain truthful, for falsehood destroys princely destiny.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Bàrà, celebrated as the sign of poetic eloquence, princely elevation, and financial breakthrough. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Era: Highly favored by court bards, royal orators, and financial treasurers (Ilari). Transatlantic Resilience: Preserved as Ogbe Bara in Santería, famous for the proverb 'A lie gives birth to a hundred lies'.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I on the right and I/II/II/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Sacrificial items include pumpkin (Ẹ̀lẹ́gẹdẹ), white rooster, and cowrie currency.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for leaders, speakers, and entrepreneurs facing economic stagnation. Prescribes truth-telling, clearing debts, and offering charity to the poor.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Irọ́ pípa kì í mú awo là; òtítọ́ inú ni Ọlọ́run ń gbé ga. (Telling falsehoods never enriches an initiate; it is inner truthfulness that the Supreme Being exalts: Enforcing absolute honesty in speech.)

Ọ̀rọ̀ rere l’ẹnu awo; ẹni tí ó fọhùn ọlá kì í bẹ̀rù ọ̀tá. (Noble words flow from the lips of the initiate; he who speaks with majestic integrity fears no adversary: Celebrating the power of righteous speech.)

Ẹ̀lẹ́gẹdẹ hù lórí àtàn, ó di adé fún olówó; àìròtẹ́lẹ̀ la fi ń rí ọlá Ifá. (The humble pumpkin sprouts upon the dunghill and transforms into a crown for the wealthy; unexpectedly does the majesty of Ifá manifest: Teaching hope against social prejudice.)

title: Ogbè Ọ̀kànràn
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀kànràn.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀kànràn is the #23 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀kànràn on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Formed by pairing Ogbè with Ọ̀kànràn (directness, thunder, decisive moral confrontation). Teaches that compromise with evil is fatal; when justice is at stake, one must act with the unflinching courage of a thunderstorm.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fatunmbi, Awo Fa'lokun (1992). Iwa-Pele: Ifa Quest.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ogbè-Kànràn, embodying lightning courage, moral defiance against tyrants, and resolving judicial litigation. Imperial Era: Consulted by judicial tribunals of the Ọ̀yọ́ Mèsì to detect perjury. Diaspora Lineage: Documented in Cuban Osha as the sign of Ṣàngó's lightning judgment.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as I on the right and II/II/II/I on the left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Utilizes celts (Ẹdùn Àrá), red roosters, and consecrated ram horns.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast during severe legal litigations, false accusations, or state oppression. Channels Ṣàngó's fierce righteousness to vindicate the innocent.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kànràn sọ òtítọ́ kankan; àrá kì í kọ̀ láì fa ilẹ̀ ya lórí ibi. (Ọ̀kànràn speaks the truth unflinchingly; the thunderbolt never hesitates to strike down injustice: Praising absolute judicial courage.)
Ẹni tó bá gbé ogun ti òtítọ́, àrá yóò kọ lórí rẹ̀. (He who wages war against the truth shall have lightning crash upon his brow: Warning against persecuting the innocent.)

A kì í fi agídí jẹ oyè baba; ìwà pẹ̀lẹ́ ni a fi ń gun orí àléfà. (One does not seize ancestral chieftaincy through sheer obstinacy; it is through gentle character that one ascends the throne: Warning against stubborn pride.)

title: Ogbè Ògúndá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ògúndá.
description: Ogbè Ògúndá is the #24 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ògúndá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairing Ogbè with Ògúndá (Ògún creates/cuts path). Teaches that obstacles in life are not insurmountable dead ends, but raw materials for creative industry, hard work, and breakthrough.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Gúndá or Ogbè-Ìjọ̀ṣẹ́, governing the blacksmith's forge, path-clearing, and surgical medicine. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted by the Balógun (Generalissimo) before military campaigns. Transatlantic Resilience: Preserved as Ogbe Gunda in Cuba and Brazil as the sacred sign of Ògún conquering treacherous hurdles.
material_and_craftsmanship: Cast as I on the right and I/I/I/II on the left. Associated with iron implements, machetes (Àdá), palm oil offerings, and roasted yams for Ògún.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for engineers, surgeons, metalworkers, and individuals navigating entrenched obstacles. Prescribes propitiation of Ògún and relentless hard work.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògún l’ó ń la ọ̀nà fún awo; kò sí igbó tó le tí àdá kò lè wọ̀. (Ògún clears the highway for the initiate; there is no impenetrable jungle that the forged machete cannot pierce: Celebrating perseverance and courage.)

Ogbè gbé irin, Ògúndá la ọ̀nà ọlá; iṣẹ́ ọwọ́ la fi ń di olówó. (Ogbè takes up the iron, Ògúndá cleaves the path of majesty; it is through the labor of our hands that we achieve true wealth: Honoring honest technical labor.)

A kì í fi ojú tẹ́ńbẹ́lú alágbẹ̀dẹ; iná tó ń jó nínú àrọ ló ń ṣe adé fún ọba. (One does not despise the humble blacksmith; the fire blazing within his forge crafts the very crown upon the king's head: Elevating guild metallurgy.)

title: Ogbè Ọ̀sá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀sá.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀sá is the #25 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀sá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Combines Ogbè with Ọ̀sá (flight, spirit winds, sudden transformation). Teaches strategic retreat: running away to fight another day is not cowardice, but supreme tactical wisdom.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle; Washington, Teresa N. (2005). Our Mothers, Our Powers, Our Texts.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Ríkúsá (Ogbè Sees Death and Escapes), governing evasion of catastrophe and diplomatic relations with maternal witchcraft guilds (Àwọn Ìyàmi). Imperial Era: Consulted in times of panic or sudden invasion. Transatlantic Survival: Major sign in Lucumí tradition for placating the spiritual Mothers.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as I on the right and II/I/I/I on the left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Involves eggs, honey, palm oil, and red feathers offered to the cosmic Mothers.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when someone is surrounded by overwhelming adversaries or nocturnal spiritual attacks. Commands deep respect for elderly women and maternal ancestors.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè rí ikú, ó sá fún ọ̀rọ̀ ayé; àkókò la fi ń mọ bí a ṣe ń ṣe. (Ogbè beheld death and took flight to preserve life; it is by reading the times that one knows how to act: Validating tactical retreat.)
Bí a bá bọwọ̀ fún àwọn Ìyá wa, a ó rí àlàáfíà gbé ayé. (If we accord due reverence to our primordial Mothers, we shall dwell in enduring peace: Demanding respect for feminine cosmic power.)

Ẹni tó sá fún ogun yóò tún wá jà ní ọ̀la; a kì í kú lásán sí ojú ogun. (He who flees from today's ambush shall live to fight tomorrow; one does not perish needlessly on the field of battle: Exhorting self-preservation.)

title: Ogbè Ìká
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ìká.
description: Ogbè Ìká is the #26 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ìká on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairing Ogbè with Ìká (wickedness, coiling serpent, finger of accusation). Teaches that the ultimate antidote to malice is moral composure; the righteous person must not mirror the evil tactics of adversaries.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Ká, governing self-control, surviving toxic conspiracies, and subduing malicious gossip. Imperial Era: Consulted when internal treason or poison was suspected in royal palaces. Diaspora Preservation: Preserved in Cuba as the sign of neutralizing venom through patience.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I on the right and II/I/II/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Employs cooling herbs, shea butter (Òrí), and white pigeons to pacify hot temperaments.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when an innocent person is encircled by slanderers, backbiters, or malicious conspirators. Prescribes calm silence and ritual purification.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìká kì í jẹ́ kí ilé awo bàjẹ́; sùúrù la fi ń pa ibi run. (Malice shall never destroy the house of the initiate; it is through patient endurance that evil is extinguished: Teaching moral triumph over hatred.)
Ẹni tó ń gbin èébú yóò kórè ìbànújẹ́; a kì í fi ibi san ibi. (He who sows insult shall reap sorrow; one does not repay evil with evil: Enforcing ethical conduct under provocation.)

Ejò kì í bímọ kí ó fi ọmọ rẹ̀ jọ ẹja; ìwà rere ni àmì ọmọ lúwàbí. (The serpent never gives birth and expects its offspring to resemble a fish; virtuous conduct is the indelible sign of the well-born child: Reaffirming moral pedigree.)

title: Ogbè Òtúúrúpọ̀n
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Òtúúrúpọ̀n.
description: Ogbè Òtúúrúpọ̀n is the #27 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Òtúúrúpọ̀n on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Combines Ogbè with Òtúúrúpọ̀n (carrying weight on the back, maternal bearing). Teaches that true leadership is caretaking: true honor consists in bearing the burdens of the vulnerable and rearing righteous children.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ogbè-Tọmọpọ̀n (Ogbè Carries the Child on the Back), governing pregnancy, pediatrics, and family nurturing. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal birthings and succession blessings. Transatlantic Lineage: Documented in Cuban Ifá as the primary sign for children's health.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I on the right and II/II/I/II on the left. Involves herbal infant washes (Àgbo Ọmọ), honey, and woven carrying sashes (Ọ̀já).
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for expectant mothers, sick infants, and community leaders responsible for collective welfare. Reaffirms child-protection ethics.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè pọ̀n ọmọ sí ẹ̀yìn, ó fi ọlá bo ilé; ọmọ rere ni adé ayé. (Ogbè carries the child upon its back, clothing the household in majesty; a virtuous child is the crown of earthly life: Celebrating children as supreme blessings.)

Ẹni tó tọ́jú ọmọ kékeré ti tọ́jú ọjọ́ ọ̀la; a kì í fi ọmọ sílẹ̀ láìní ẹ̀kọ́. (He who nurtures a young child has secured the future; one does not leave a child without sound education: Mandating moral upbringing.)

Ọ̀já tó fi pọ̀n mí kò ní ya; àdúrà ìyá ni àbò tí kò lè wó. (The sash with which my mother strapped me shall never tear; a mother's blessing is a fortress that never crumbles: Honoring filial gratitude.)

title: Ogbè Òtúá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Òtúá.
description: Ogbè Òtúá is the #28 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Òtúá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairing Ogbè with Òtúá (peace, release, covenant, righteous prayer). Teaches the universal fraternity of all spiritual seekers; true religion is recognized by its fruits of peace and human kindness.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1976). Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Túá or Ogbè-Aláwùrà, governing peace treaties, divine covenant, and religious tolerance. Imperial Era: Consulted when foreign religions (such as Islam in the 17th century) interacted with Yorùbá institutions. Transatlantic Survival: Major sign in Lucumí tradition celebrating unblemished spiritual truth.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as I on the right and I/II/I/I on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Sacrifices include white doves, white chalk (Ẹfun), and pure honey.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast during treaty ratifications, inter-faith reconciliations, and prayers for personal purity. Promotes universal moral tolerance.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè tú àwọ̀n, ó fi àlàáfíà wọ ìlú; àwọn olùwà tútù ni yóò jogún ayé. (Ogbè dismantled the net of strife and entered the city with peace; it is the gentle-hearted who shall inherit the earth: Exalting peace above conquest.)

Àdúrà tí a fi ọkàn mímọ́ gbà kì í ṣubú sílẹ̀; Ọlọ́run ń gbọ́ ohùn olódodo. (The prayer offered with a pure heart never falls to the ground; the Supreme Being listens to the voice of the upright: Celebrating pure intentions.)

Bí a bá ń wá àlàáfíà, a kò gbọdọ̀ gbin ọ̀rọ̀ ìbínú; ẹnu tútù ní ń fa oríire wá. (If we seek peace, we must not plant seeds of wrath; gentle speech is that which attracts good fortune: Mandating peaceful diplomacy.)

title: Ogbè Ìrẹtẹ̀
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ìrẹtẹ̀.
description: Ogbè Ìrẹtẹ̀ is the #29 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ìrẹtẹ̀ on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Formed by pairing Ogbè with Ìrẹtẹ̀ (humility, stepping down, healing, overcoming infirmity). Teaches that true greatness emerges from the crucible of suffering; pride invites affliction, while humility invites miraculous healing.
provenance_and_citations: Abimbola, Wande (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifa; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ogbè-Ate or Ogbè-Ìrẹtẹ̀, governing the conquest of illness, skin diseases, and humiliation. Imperial Era: Consulted by court physicians dealing with contagions. Transatlantic Lineage: Documented in Cuban Osha-Ifá as the sign of Ọbalúayé (Babalú Ayé) curing infirmities through humility.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as I on the right and I/I/II/I on the left. Associated with cornmeal offerings, palm wine, guinea fowl, and medicinal baths.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for people suffering from chronic diseases, skin afflictions, or severe social humiliation. Directs devotees to humble themselves and seek spiritual hygiene.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè tẹ orí ìṣẹ́ mọ́lẹ̀, ó di olówó; ẹni tí ó ba tẹríbà fún awo yóò gbádùn. (Ogbè stepped upon the head of poverty and became wealthy; he who humbles himself before sacred wisdom shall enjoy long life: Linking humility to elevation.)

Àrùn kì í pa ẹni tí Ifá ń gbé; ìwòsàn dé fún ẹni tí ó tẹríba. (Disease cannot slay the soul whom Ifá upholds; healing arrives for him who bows with a humble heart: Praising spiritual recovery through humility.)

A kì í fi ìgbéraga wọlé ọba; ẹni tí ó gbọ́n ní ń fi ẹ̀rọ̀ gbé orí rẹ̀ ga. (One does not enter the king's palace in arrogance; the wise person elevates his head through gentle composure: Teaching modesty before authority.)

title: Ogbè Ọ̀ṣẹ́
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Ọ̀ṣẹ́.
description: Ogbè Ọ̀ṣẹ́ is the #30 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ogbè on the right with Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (radiance, victory over shame, golden sweetness) on the left. Known as Ogbè-Ṣẹ́, teaching that perseverance through poverty inevitably leads to triumphant distinction.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.
historical_timeline: Employed by young apprentices and market women throughout the coastal trade ports of Badagry, Lagos, and Porto-Novo to secure commercial triumph against monopolistic cartels.
material_and_craftsmanship: Right column: I I I I; Left column: I II I II; drawn alongside pure honeycomb and sweet spring water upon carved divination boards.
social_and_ritual_context: Consulted by individuals seeking elevation, love, or commercial success, prescribing sweet offerings to Ọ̀ṣun and the ancestors.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Oyin kì í korò lẹ́nu ọmọdé; Ogbè Ṣẹ́ ló ń sọ ayé di dídùn. (Honey is never bitter in the mouth of a child; it is Ogbè Ṣẹ́ that transforms existence into radiant sweetness: Teaching that joy follows perseverance.)

Ẹni tó bá ní sùúrù yóò jẹ oyin orí àpáta; ayọ̀ ń bọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìpọ́njú. (He who possesses steadfast patience shall eat rich honey from the face of the barren rock; triumphant joy always follows hardship: Inspiring hopeful resilience.)
diaspora_connections: Known in Cuba as Ogbe She, an auspicious sign directly linked to Oshún, beauty, wealth, and sweet fortune.
media_production_notes: Golden honey dripping over amber beads in warm sunlight, accompanied by gentle river water flowing over polished stones.

title: Ogbè Òfún
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ogbè with the qualities of Òfún.
description: Ogbè Òfún is the #31 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ogbè on the right and Òfún on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ogbè on the right with Òfún (divine grace, white purity, miraculous salvation) on the left. Known as Ogbè-Fún, representing the synthesis of the first and sixteenth kings, bridging dawn and completion.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.
historical_timeline: Invoked at the most solemn purification ceremonies of the imperial palaces of Ọ̀yọ́ and Ifẹ̀ during constitutional transition rites.
material_and_craftsmanship: Right column: I I I I; Left column: II I II I; drawn with sacred white chalk (Ẹfun) and lead ornaments upon consecrated shrines.
social_and_ritual_context: Consulted in catastrophic crises where all material hope is exhausted; represents divine intervention and miraculous preservation.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ogbè Fún fún ni ní ẹ̀mí, ó fún ni ní àlàáfíà; ẹfun funfun kì í ba aṣọ jẹ́. (Ogbè Fún bestows life and bestows tranquil peace; pure white chalk never defiles clean cloth: Teaching unblemished spiritual purity.)

Bí gbogbo ayé bá dí mọ́ ni, Ogbè Fún ló ń la ọ̀nà; àṣẹ Ọlọ́run kì í yẹ̀. (When all earthly paths seem shuttered, it is Ogbè Fún that carves an open highway; the divine decree never falters: Affirming miraculous providence.)
diaspora_connections: Known as Ogbe Fun in Santería as a sacred sign of Obatalá, demanding absolute white purity and moral rectitude.
media_production_notes: An assembly of initiates dressed in pristine white woven robes stepping silently into the morning light of a temple sanctuary.

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ogbè
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ogbè.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ogbè is the #32 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ogbè on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right (shadow, transition) with Ogbè on the left (light, renewal). Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bì-Ogbè, representing resurrection: light bursting out of deepest darkness.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination.
historical_timeline: Consulted during ancient famines, pestilences, or civil crises where rebirth of the commonwealth was desperately required.
material_and_craftsmanship: Right column: II II II II; Left column: I I I I; inscribed across two contrasting halves of the Ọpọ́n Ifá tray.
social_and_ritual_context: Marks the miraculous revival of dying lineages, recovery from terminal ailments, and political rebirth after catastrophic war.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Nínú òkùnkùn ni ìmọ́lẹ̀ ti ń yọ; Ọ̀yẹ̀kú bì Ogbè kì í jẹ́ kí ayé parun. (Out of the darkest void does radiant light emerge; Ọ̀yẹ̀kú bì Ogbè never permits creation to perish: Teaching hope in times of deep despair.)

Ẹni tó subú kì í dúró sílẹ̀; àtúnṣe ni Ifá ń gbé wá fún gbogbo ayé. (He who falls does not remain permanently upon the ground; restorative renewal is what Ifá brings to the entire universe: Proclaiming redemption.)
diaspora_connections: Revered as Oyekun Bedura in Cuban Ifá as a triumphant sign of resurrection, recovery from critical illness, and victory over death.
media_production_notes: Slow cinematic dawn where deep indigo darkness gradually dissolves as a blazing golden sunrise floods the misty landscape.

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìwòrì
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ìwòrì.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìwòrì is the #33 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ìwòrì on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Formed by pairing Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, mortality, ancestral boundary) on the right and Ìwòrì (deep spiritual vision, retrospection) on the left of Ọpọ́n Ifá. Dialectically balances dark existential fear with calm inner contemplation, demonstrating that ancestral wisdom dissipates spiritual confusion.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity (c. 9th–12th Century CE): Codified as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Wèyìn, teaching deep introspection during times of crisis. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́ Period (14th–18th Century CE): Consulted by palace counselors during dynastic transitions to uncover hidden grievances. Transatlantic Survival: Preserved in Cuban and Brazilian Ifá archives as Oyekun Bori, guiding initiates through spiritual cleansing and warding off premature demise.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed upon Ọpọ́n Ifá in two vertical columns: double strokes (II) on the right for Ọ̀yẹ̀kú and II/I/I/II on the left for Ìwòrì. Utilizes Ewé Ọ̀dúndún and Ewé Tètè in cool spring water to calm feverish delirium.
social_and_ritual_context: Divined when a family is haunted by unresolved ancestral disputes or recurring nightmares. Prescribes ethical reconciliation among kin and propitiation of ancestral spirits.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú wòrì wò awo, awo wò Ọ̀yẹ̀kú; a kì í fi ojú tẹ́ńbẹ́lú àṣẹ àwọn àgbà. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú gazes into the initiate and the initiate gazes into Ọ̀yẹ̀kú; one must never look with disdain upon the sovereign decree of the ancestral elders: Teaching mutual spiritual reverence between seer and cosmos.)

Bí òru bá kù sẹ́yìn, ojúmọ́ ìmọ̀ a mọ́; a kì í bẹ̀rù òkùnkùn tí a bá ní àbọ̀ Ifá. (Though the night lingers, the dawn of enlightenment inevitably breaks; one harbors no fear of the dark when sheltered by Ifá: Encouraging perseverance through crisis.)
Ìwòrì tẹ ojú ẹjọ́ mọ́lẹ̀; àwọn olùfẹ́ òtítọ́ ní ń rí àlàáfíà Ọlọ́run. (Ìwòrì stamps out the seeds of dispute; lovers of truth are those who inherit divine peace: Prioritizing truthful mediation.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òdí
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Òdí.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òdí is the #34 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Òdí on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (mortal vulnerability) with Òdí (rampart, womb, protective barrier). Teaches that mortal dangers can be nullified by constructing impenetrable ethical and spiritual boundaries.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Dí, governing defensive fortresses, sealing boundaries against epidemic contagions, and maternal preservation. Imperial Era: Consulted before town walls and moats were consecrated. Diaspora Lineage: Retained in Lucumí patakís as Oyekun Di, celebrated for preventing spiritual invasions.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as II on the right and I/II/II/I on the left. Involves consecrated black soap enriched with snail fluid (Ìgbín) and Ewé Ètìpọ́nlà to fortify the human aura.
social_and_ritual_context: Employed to protect pregnant mothers, ward off sorcery, and seal property against boundary encroachments.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú dí ojú ikú, ó ti ọ̀nà àrùn; ilé tí a fi àṣẹ dí kì í gbọ́ orin ọ̀fọ̀. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú barricades the path of death and shuts the gate against disease; a household sealed with sacred authority hears no mourning dirges: Proclaiming divine immunity from catastrophe.)

Odi tí a mọ pẹ̀lú sùúrù kì í wó; awo tó mọ ìwà rẹ̀ kì í tẹ́. (A rampart erected with patient labor never crumbles; an initiate conscious of his character never stumbles into disgrace: Emphasizing patience in building defenses.)

Ẹni tí ó fẹ́ dí àpò kò gbọ́dọ̀ bínú sí abẹ́rẹ́; pẹ̀lẹ́pẹ̀lẹ́ la fi ń rán aṣọ ọlá. (He who seeks to stitch closed the leaking pouch must not quarrel with the needle; it is with steady care that robes of majesty are tailored: Valuing delicate tools and diplomacy.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ìrosùn.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn is the #35 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ìrosùn on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Synthesis of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness, ancestral transition) and Ìrosùn (scarlet camwood, circulatory vitality, ancestral sleep). Teaches that hereditary darkness is transfigured into honor through ancestral blood veneration and truth.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Rosùn, governing lineage purification, ancestral camwood consecration, and unveiling subterranean treasures. Imperial Era: Invoked during royal investitures to clear ancestral curses from the royal lineage. Transatlantic Preservation: Documented in Cuban Ifá as Oyekun Koso, an oracle for reversing sudden misfortune.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and I/I/II/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Mixed with Osùn (camwood powder) and Ewé Ìyàlódé, utilizing sacrificial sheep or roosters.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when a seeker faces unexplainable family stagnation or hereditary circulatory ailments. Directs initiates to appease paternal forebears.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú rosùn lójú awo, ìbànújẹ́ yipada sí ayọ̀; orí rere kì í gbé inú òkùnkùn pẹ́. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú anoints itself with camwood before the initiate, turning sorrow into radiant joy; good destiny never lingers long in darkness: Announcing imminent relief after grief.)

Ẹ̀jẹ̀ kì í da awo lójú; orísun tí kò gbẹ la ti ń mu omi ọlá. (Lineage blood never deceives the true initiate; it is from an inexhaustible fountain that we drink the water of nobility: Celebrating the enduring power of ancestral bloodlines.)

A kì í fi osùn pa aró run; olúkúlùkù àwọ̀ ló ní ibi tí ó wọ̀. (One does not use red camwood to destroy blue indigo; every distinct color has its rightful station: Teaching diversity and social respect.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀wọ́nrín
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ọ̀wọ́nrín.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀wọ́nrín is the #36 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ọ̀wọ́nrín on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (dark stagnation) with Ọ̀wọ́nrín (whirlwind, sudden commerce, scarcity). Teaches that the turbulence of poverty is quelled by unexpected spiritual windfalls when moral integrity is maintained.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fatunmbi, Awo Fa'lokun (1992). Iwa-Pele: Ifa Quest.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Wọ́nrín, dealing with unexpected trade windfalls, sudden reversals of fortune, and maritime commerce along coastal lagoons. Imperial Era: Consulted by merchants traversing the Niger trade routes. Diaspora Survival: Preserved in Brazilian Candomblé and Cuban Santería as Oyekun Wonrin.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as II on the right and II/II/I/I on the left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Utilizes Ewé Ọ́kìkà, Ewé Ṣaworo-pẹ́pẹ́, and offerings of honey and bananas to appease wind deities.
social_and_ritual_context: Divined during economic instability, sudden business loss, or turbulent community unrest. Prescribes generosity and emergency savings.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀wọ́nrín gba Ọ̀yẹ̀kú sílẹ̀ lọ́wọ́ ìpọ́njú; afẹ́fẹ́ kì í fẹ́ kí ó gbé àpáta lọ. (Ọ̀wọ́nrín rescues Ọ̀yẹ̀kú from hardship; the fiercest whirlwind never blows so hard as to dislodge an immovable granite rock: Affirming foundational stability against adversity.)
Owó kì í wá láì sí làálàá; awo tó mọ iṣẹ́ ṣe kì í ráhùn ebi. (Wealth never arrives without honest exertion; an initiate master of his craft never laments of starvation: Demanding rigorous industry.)

Bí ìjì bá ń jà, a kì í gun orí igi; sùúrù la fi ń dúró de ìmọ́lẹ̀. (When the tempest rages, one does not climb the canopy of the trees; it is with patience that one awaits the return of daylight: Warning against rash actions during crises.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀bàrà
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ọ̀bàrà.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀bàrà is the #37 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ọ̀bàrà on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (gloom, mortification) with Ọ̀bàrà (manifestation, royal abundance, eloquence). Teaches that patient truth-telling dismantles false accusations and converts humble poverty into royal dignity.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bàrà, celebrated as the chapter of unexpected royal vindication, poetic speech, and overcoming slander. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Favored by royal heralds (Ilari) confronting conspiracies. Diaspora Resilience: Maintained in Lucumí tradition as Oyekun Bara for averting public disgrace.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and I/II/II/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Sacrificial elements include Ewé Ẹ̀lẹ́gẹdẹ (pumpkin leaves), rooster, and white cowrie shells.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for leaders whose integrity is attacked by court rumors. Prescribes truthful public discourse, settlement of debts, and inner fortitude.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú bàrà sọ òtítọ́ ọ̀rọ̀; ẹnu awo ni àṣẹ Ọlọ́run ti ń jáde. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀bàrà speaks the unvarnished truth; from the mouth of the initiate the sovereign decree of the Creator flows: Emphasizing the sanctity of prophetic speech.)

Ẹni tí ayé kẹ́gàn ní àná ló ń jẹ ọba lónìí; àìròtẹ́lẹ̀ ni Ifá ń gbé olódodo ga. (He whom the world mocked yesterday is the one crowned as king today; unexpectedly does Ifá exalt the upright: Warning against underestimating the humble.)

A kì í fi irọ́ kọ́ ààfin; òtítọ́ inú nìkan ló lè gbé adé dúró lórí. (One does not erect a royal palace upon falsehood; only inner truthfulness can sustain the crown upon the head: Demanding ethical governance.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀kànràn
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ọ̀kànràn.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀kànràn is the #38 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ọ̀kànràn on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Combines Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (death) and Ọ̀kànràn (thunder, decisive moral courage). Expresses the dialectical triumph of raw moral courage over intimidation; standing firm against existential bullies neutralizes their power.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Barnes, Sandra T. (1997). Africa's Ogun: Old World and New.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Pèkú (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Calls Death to Halt), embodying lightning defiance against malevolent hexes. Imperial Era: Consulted during judicial trials by ordeal. Transatlantic Retention: Documented in Cuban Osha-Ifá as Oyekun Foloko Kana.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked as II on the right and II/II/II/I on the left on Ìyẹ̀rosùn. Utilizes Ẹdùn Àrá (meteorite thunderstone), Ewé Ìná, and ram offerings to Ṣàngó.
social_and_ritual_context: Invoked in intense legal battles, false incarcerations, or sudden violent intimidation. Calls down judicial vindication.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú kànràn, ikú yẹra; àrá kì í kọ lórí olódodo tí kò dẹ́ṣẹ̀. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀kànràn strikes, and death retreats; thunder never strikes down an upright man who has committed no transgression: Assuring divine protection for the blameless.)

Bí a bá ń ja fún ẹ̀tọ́, a kì í bẹ̀rù ariwo ọ̀tá; ọkàn líle la fi ń gbẹ́jọ́ kàlẹ̀. (When fighting for justice, one does not tremble at the clamor of the adversary; it is with stout heart that one presents one's case: Encouraging fearless integrity.)

Àpọ́nlé ni a fi ń wo àgbà; ẹni tó rúbọ Ọ̀kànràn kì í dáràn nílé ẹjọ́. (It is with reverence that one honors elders; he who offers the sacrifice of Ọ̀kànràn never meets ruin in the court of law: Commending humility before ancestral judges.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ògúndá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ògúndá.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ògúndá is the #39 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ògúndá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Synthesis of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (peril of death) and Ògúndá (Ògún's creative cleaving). Teaches that through courageous decisive intervention and technological craft, fatal obstacles are cut down.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Gúndá, governing the surgeon's scalpel, the blacksmith's forge, and battlefield clearing. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted by warrior guilds before military deployments. Transatlantic Diaspora: Maintained in Cuban Ifá as Oyekun Tekunda for surgical protection.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and I/I/I/II on the left. Associated with forged iron implements, Ewé Pèrègún, palm oil, and roasted yam offerings.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast before surgical operations, hazardous long-distance travel, or large-scale construction projects. Secures Ògún's protection.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ògún yọ Ọ̀yẹ̀kú nínú ewu; irin kì í bẹ̀rù igbó tó kún fún ẹ̀gún. (Ògún extricates Ọ̀yẹ̀kú from imminent danger; forged iron harbors no fear of the briar-choked jungle: Celebrating technological and spiritual breakthroughs.)

Ẹni tí ó mú ọ̀bẹ Ògún kò gbọ́dọ̀ bínú láìnídìí; àṣejù ní ń bí àbùkù. (He who wields the consecrated blade of Ògún must not flare into senseless rage; excess passion only generates disgrace: Restraining power with self-discipline.)

Bí a bá fẹ́ là ọ̀nà ọlá, iṣẹ́ agbára la fi ń bẹ̀rẹ̀; kò sí àṣeyọrí fún ọ̀lẹ. (If we desire to clear the pathway of majesty, strenuous labor is the starting point; there is no victory for the slothful: Exhorting physical diligence.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀sá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ọ̀sá.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀sá is the #40 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ọ̀sá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (dark menace) with Ọ̀sá (flight, spirit winds, sudden transition). Teaches tactical retreat: withdrawing to regroup preserves life and ensures final victory.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Lawal, Babatunde (1996). The Gelede Spectacle; Washington, Teresa N. (2005). Our Mothers, Our Powers, Our Texts.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bìsá, governing strategic flight from catastrophe and placating nocturnal astral societies. Imperial Era: Invoked during sudden military invasions to execute orderly evacuations. Diaspora Preservation: Documented in Lucumí Ifá as Oyekun Sa.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as II on the right and II/I/I/I on the left. Involves eggs, honey, Ewé Ọ̀jìjí, and red feather offerings to the primordial Mothers.
social_and_ritual_context: Divined when a seeker is encircled by hostile conspiracies or supernatural panic. Recommends quiet withdrawal and maternal appeasement.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú sá fún ibi, ó bọ́ sí àbò àwọn Ìyá; ẹni tí àwọn àgbàlagbà bá tì lẹ́yìn kì í kú. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú fled from evil and found refuge beneath the mantle of the Mothers; he whom the elder matriarchs endorse shall never perish: Commending peace with feminine spiritual forces.)

Ẹyẹ kì í fò kí ó gbàgbé ilẹ̀; bí a bá rìn jìnnà tó, orísun la ó padà sí. (The bird never flies so far as to forget the earth below; however far we roam, to our ancestral origin we must return: Teaching loyalty to one's roots.)

Bí afẹ́fẹ́ bá ń fẹ́, a kì í fi iná sí etí koríko; ìṣọ́ra ni baba àlàáfíà. (When strong winds blow, one does not kindle a flame near dry thatch; caution is the father of enduring peace: Preaching prevention over reaction.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìká
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ìká.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìká is the #41 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ìká on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (shadow of transition) with Ìká (restraint, coiling venom). Teaches that the poison of hatred cannot cure hatred; only absolute moral self-mastery neutralizes treachery.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bìká, governing the neutralizing of toxic poisons, coiling vipers, and malevolent sorcery. Imperial Era: Consulted in court when food poisoning of royalty was suspected. Diaspora Lineage: Retained in Cuban Ifá as Oyekun Bika.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and II/I/II/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with cooling shea butter (Òrí), Ewé Ègé, and white pigeon sacrifice.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when someone is surrounded by slanderous backbiters or suspicious domestic poisoning. Prescribes calm discretion and detoxifying herbal washes.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú ká ọwọ́ ibi kúrò lórí awo; ẹni tó fẹ́ gbẹ́ kòtò fún ẹlòmíràn yóò wọ̀ ọ́. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú coils back the hand of evil from the initiate; he who digs a pit for another shall fall into it himself: Enforcing cosmic retribution upon conspirators.)

Ìkà kò mọ̀ pé Ọlọ́run ń wo ilẹ̀; ìwà rere ni àbò tí kò lè wó. (The wicked conspirator forgets that the Creator surveys the earth; righteous character is an indestructible fortress: Warning against deceit.)

A kì í fi ọwọ́ méjèèjì gba ejò sí abíyá; awo tó fojú fò kì í jẹ oró. (One does not fold both arms to nurse a viper into one's bosom; an alert initiate never tastes bitter venom: Demanding strict boundary-setting.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òtúúrúpọ̀n
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Òtúúrúpọ̀n.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òtúúrúpọ̀n is the #42 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Òtúúrúpọ̀n on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (threat of mortality) and Òtúúrúpọ̀n (carrying on the back, maternal care). Teaches that tender parental nurturing and communal responsibility preserve the human race against extinction.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Fadipe, N.A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Codified as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bàtúrúpọ̀n, governing infant health, safe delivery, and protecting expectant mothers from mortality. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal pregnancies. Transatlantic Survival: Revered in Cuba as Oyekun Batrupon for pediatric preservation.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as II on the right and II/II/I/II on the left. Involves herbal washes (Àgbo Ọmọ) made of Ewé Àbáwẹ̀, snail broth, and baby-carrying wraps.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for sickly children, women facing difficult childbirth, or institutions bearing heavy civic responsibilities. Strengthens child welfare.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú pọ̀n ọmọ mọ́ra, Ikú kò rí i mú; ọmọ lúwàbí kì í sọnu lábẹ́ ìyá. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú clasps the child tightly to its back, and Death is denied its prize; a noble child never perishes in the embrace of its mother: Celebrating maternal protection over life.)

Ẹrù tí a fi sùúrù gbé kì í pa ni lára; àṣeyọrí ń dúró de ẹni tí kò rẹ̀wẹ̀sì. (A burden shouldered with patience never fractures the spine; victory awaits the spirit that refuses despair: Exhorting resilience.)

A kì í fi ọmọ ọlọ́mọ bọ Òrìṣà; ìdájọ́ òdodo ni ìpìlẹ̀ ayé. (One does not sacrifice another's child to a deity; impartial justice is the cornerstone of the universe: Forbidding the exploitation of the weak.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òtúá
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Òtúá.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òtúá is the #43 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Òtúá on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (existential shadows) with Òtúá (peace, prayer, release). Teaches that peace is not passive absence of conflict, but active spiritual liberation from fear through sacred covenant.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Túá, governing the clearing of dark shadows through spiritual light, covenant oaths, and religious tolerance. Imperial Era: Consulted when establishing diplomatic treaties between neighboring kingdoms. Diaspora Lineage: Maintained as Oyekun Otura in Cuban Ifá.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and I/II/I/I on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with pure honey, white chalk (Ẹfun), and white dove sacrifice.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast during treaty ratifications, inter-family reconciliations, and prayers for freedom from spiritual torment.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú tú àbùkù dànù, ó fi àlàáfíà wọlé; ẹni tí ó ba bá Ifá rìn kì í rìn nínú òkùnkùn. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú casts off all disgrace and enters the home in peace; he who walks beside Ifá never wanders in the dark: Exalting spiritual light.)

Àlà tí a fi wọ awo kì í dọ̀tí; ìwà mímọ́ ni ẹ̀ṣọ́ ọkàn. (The pristine white cloth worn by the initiate must never be soiled; pure character is the jewel of the soul: Demanding immaculate personal ethics.)

Ọ̀rọ̀ tútù ní ń pa iná ìbínú; a kì í fi ìjà yanjú ọ̀rọ̀ àgbà. (Gentle speech extinguishes the blazing fire of wrath; one does not resolve elder disputes through violence: Promoting diplomatic dialogue.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrẹtẹ̀
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ìrẹtẹ̀.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrẹtẹ̀ is the #44 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ìrẹtẹ̀ on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (peril of the flesh) with Ìrẹtẹ̀ (humility, earth, physical convalescence). Teaches that physical healing begins when human pride bows before ancestral medicine and natural laws.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Verger, Pierre (1995). Ewé: The Use of Plants in Yoruba Society.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Rẹtẹ̀, celebrated for curing persistent skin contagions, leprosy, and humiliating infirmities. Imperial Era: Consulted by herbalist guilds serving isolation wards. Diaspora Preservation: Documented in Cuban Osha-Ifá as Oyekun Birete under Babalú Ayé.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as II on the right and I/I/II/I on the left. Involves Ewé Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ewé Gbégbé, corn flour (Ẹ̀kọ), and offerings to Ọbalúayé.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast for sufferers of chronic dermatological afflictions, bone pain, or societal ostracization. Commands absolute hygiene and humility.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú rẹtẹ̀ mọ́lẹ̀, ó gbé ìlera wá; àrùn kì í kọjá àṣẹ Olódùmarè. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú bowed low in humility and brought forth vibrant health; no infirmity can supersede the mandate of the Almighty: Affirming divine healing over stubborn afflictions.)
Ẹni tí ó tẹríba kì í kọsẹ̀ láé; ìgbéraga ní ń mú ìṣubú wá. (He who bows his head in humility never stumbles into ruin; it is arrogant pride that invites downfall: Praising modest self-restraint.)

Ìwòsàn dé fún ẹni tó mọ̀ àṣà rẹ̀; a kì í ta orísun wa nù láti jẹun. (Healing arrives for him who honors his ancestral tradition; one does not sell off one's roots to buy fleeting bread: Urging cultural faithfulness.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀ṣẹ́
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Ọ̀ṣẹ́.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ọ̀ṣẹ́ is the #45 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Conjunction of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (sorrow, mourning) and Ọ̀ṣẹ́ (sweetness, victory, feminine grace). Teaches that sorrow is temporary; when approached with sweet offerings and moral beauty, life blossoms anew.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Abiodun, Rowland (2014). Yoruba Art and Language.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Ṣẹ́, governing the dissolution of grief through feminine beauty, wealth, and riverine blessings. Imperial Era: Consulted during royal festivals to banish mourning from palaces. Diaspora Retention: Maintained in Cuban Ifá as Oyekun She under Ọ̀ṣun.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II on the right and I/II/I/II on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with Ewé Àjẹ́obàlé, river water, brass ornaments, and honey for Ọ̀ṣun.
social_and_ritual_context: Divined for seekers suffering long periods of sorrow, depression, or reproductive barrenness. Restores joy and fertility.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú ṣẹ́gun ọ̀tá, ó rí ayọ̀ Ọ̀ṣun; omi kì í bá oríire jà. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú vanquished the adversary and discovered the sweet joy of Ọ̀ṣun; running water never quarrels with auspicious fortune: Celebrating joyous breakthrough.)

Ẹni tó fi oyin bọ Ifá kì í fẹ́nú kora; adùn ayé ń bọ̀ lẹ́yìn ìpọ́njú. (He who propitiates Ifá with honey shall never taste bitterness; the sweetness of life arrives after the season of toil: Giving comfort during hardship.)

Bí a bá ń wẹ àbùkù dànù, a kì í fi ẹrọ̀fọ̀ pa ojú; ìmọ́tótó ni baba ìgbéga. (When washing away dishonor, one does not splash mud upon the face; cleanliness of deed is the father of elevation: Enforcing spotless integrity.)

title: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òfún
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú with the qualities of Òfún.
description: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Òfún is the #46 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and Òfún on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (darkness) with Òfún (divine white creation, Ọbàtálá). Encapsulates the profound philosophical truth of resurrection: from the deepest abyss of winter, eternal dawn is born.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1976). Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Idowu, E. Bolaji (1962). Olodumare: God in Yoruba Belief.
historical_timeline: Classical Antiquity: Known as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Fún or Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-Bàfún, the supreme mystery where death is swallowed by transcendent light. Imperial Era: Revered by royal elders as the sign of peaceful longevity. Diaspora Survival: Preserved in Lucumí Ifá as Oyekun Berduni / Oyekun Fun.
material_and_craftsmanship: Marked on Ìyẹ̀rosùn as II on the right and II/I/II/I on the left. Involves pristine white pigeons, Ẹfun (chalk), Ewé Ọ̀bàtálá, and shea butter.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast during grave medical crises where hope seems lost. Reconnects the patient directly to Ọbàtálá's primordial breath of life.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú fún funfun gba ayé, Ikú sá fún ìmọ́lẹ̀ Ọbàtálá. (Ọ̀yẹ̀kú shone in immaculate white and reclaimed the world; Death fled before the radiance of Ọbàtálá: Proclaiming the triumph of divine grace over the grave.)

Àlà funfun kì í bẹ̀rù aró; ẹni tí Ọlọ́run bá kọ́ kò lè bàjẹ́. (Pure white linen harbors no fear of the dye vat; he whom the Creator has built up cannot be pulled down: Affirming inviolable spiritual protection.)

Ẹni tí ó ru ẹbọ Òfún ti la ibi kọjá; orí rere ni apata tí kì í yẹ̀. (He who offers the sacrifice of Òfún has transcended all calamity; a well-aligned destiny is an unshakeable shield: Emphasizing spiritual alignment.)

title: Ìwòrì Ogbè
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ìwòrì with the qualities of Ogbè.
description: Ìwòrì Ogbè is the #47 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ìwòrì on the right and Ogbè on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ìwòrì (deep spiritual sight) on the right with Ogbè (pristine cosmic radiance) on the left. Demonstrates that intuitive perception combined with luminous truth removes all blindness and confusion.
provenance_and_citations: Abímbọ́lá, Wándé (1975). Sixteen Great Poems of Ifá; Bascom, William (1969). Ifa Divination; Epega, A.A. & Neimark, P. (1995). The Sacred Ifa Oracle.
historical_timeline: Classical Ilé-Ifẹ̀ Antiquity: Known as Ìwòrì-Bogbè or Ìwòrì-Gbé, celebrated for illuminating dark mysteries, exposing concealed thefts, and bestowing clear vision. Imperial Ọ̀yọ́: Consulted by judges before delivering capital sentences. Transatlantic Lineage: Renowned across Cuba and Brazil as Iwori Bogbe.
material_and_craftsmanship: Inscribed as II/I/I/II on the right and I on the left on Ọpọ́n Ifá. Prepared with morning dew water, Ewé Ọ̀yọ́yọ́, and white rooster offerings.
social_and_ritual_context: Cast when mystery veils an important civic matter, or when an innocent person is wrongfully suspected of crime. Clears moral ambiguity.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ìwòrì bogbè tan ìmọ́lẹ̀ sí gbogbo igbó; ohun tí ó pamọ́ kò lè sọnù mọ́. (Ìwòrì Ogbè radiates illumination across the deep forest; that which was hidden can no longer remain concealed: Celebrating the revelation of truth.)

Ojú awo kì í fọ́ sí ojú ọ̀ràn; ìmọ̀ tó jinlẹ̀ ló ń yan ìdájọ́. (The spiritual eye of the initiate is never blinded by confusing circumstances; deep wisdom alone arbitrates justice: Teaching clear judicial vision.)

Bí ìmọ́lẹ̀ bá dé, àwọn alákọ̀kọ̀ a tẹríba; a kì í fi òtítọ́ sọfọ. (When light arrives, the schemers bow their heads; one never mourns while standing upon truth: Exalting the victory of righteousness.)

title: Ìwòrì Ọ̀yẹ̀kú
cosmological_meaning: Harmonizes the principles of Ìwòrì with the qualities of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú.
description: Ìwòrì Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is the #48 chapter of the 256 Odù Ifá, formed by combining Ìwòrì on the right and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the left of the Ọpọ́n Ifá.
etymology_and_philosophy: Pairs Ìwòrì (spiritual investigation) with Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (ancestral realm). Teaches that by reverently investigating the deeds of departed ancestors, living generations avoid repeating catastrophic historical errors.
